subtopic_detail: Rings and linear furrows seen at endoscopy for a food bolus obstruction in a young man with atopy and no biopsies taken
stem:
You are the gastroenterology registrar reviewing a 24 year old man the morning after an emergency endoscopy for a steak bolus that had been stuck for four hours. The bolus was pushed through and he is now eating without difficulty.

On questioning he tells you he has cut steak and crusty bread out of his diet over the past two years, always drinks water with meals and is usually the last to finish. He has asthma, hay fever and childhood eczema. The endoscopy report describes concentric rings and fine longitudinal furrows through the whole oesophagus, with no stricture, no ulceration and no mass, and records that no biopsies were taken.

data_table.Examination: Well and comfortable, body mass index 23 kg per square metre, abdomen soft and non tender, no cervical lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count shows an eosinophil count of 0.7 x10^9/L (0.0 to 0.5), urea creatinine and electrolytes within normal limits, C reactive protein within normal limits, endoscopy reports concentric rings and linear furrows throughout the oesophagus with no stricture, ulceration or mass and no biopsies taken

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Start a proton pump inhibitor and review his symptoms in eight weeks
options.rationale: Acid suppression is a legitimate treatment for this condition, but starting it before biopsies are taken suppresses the mucosal eosinophilia and can make the histology uninterpretable for months. Treatment follows the tissue diagnosis rather than preceding it. (Source: GESA: Eosinophilic oesophagitis clinical update)

options.text: Arrange a barium swallow and review once the study has been reported
options.rationale: Contrast radiology can show a narrowed or ringed oesophagus but cannot establish a diagnosis that is defined histologically, and the endoscopic appearance is already known. It adds a step without answering the question. (Source: GESA: Eosinophilic oesophagitis clinical update)

options.text: Repeat endoscopy and biopsy the proximal and distal oesophagus
options.rationale: The diagnosis rests on finding at least 15 eosinophils per high power field, and because the infiltrate is patchy, multiple biopsies from both the proximal and distal oesophagus are needed rather than distal samples alone. Endoscopic appearances of rings and furrows are suggestive but are neither sensitive nor specific enough to diagnose or exclude the condition. (Source: GESA: Eosinophilic oesophagitis clinical update)

options.text: Arrange oesophageal manometry and review once it has been reported
options.rationale: Manometry investigates a motility disorder, which would present with dysphagia to liquids as well as solids rather than with solid food impaction and dietary adaptation. Motility abnormalities can occur here but do not define the disease. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Eosinophilic oesophagitis)

options.text: Start a topical corticosteroid and review his symptoms in eight weeks
options.rationale: Swallowed topical corticosteroid is effective first line therapy once the diagnosis is confirmed, but giving it first removes the histological evidence needed to confirm it. The near pair here is that this becomes the right answer at the visit after the biopsies return. (Source: GESA: Eosinophilic oesophagitis clinical update)

explanation.summary: Eosinophilic oesophagitis is now the commonest cause of food bolus obstruction in young adults, and the history is typically one of years of silent adaptation, with patients cutting out meat and bread, chewing excessively, drinking with every mouthful and eating slowly, long before they present acutely. Most patients have a personal or family history of atopy, and a peripheral eosinophilia is common but neither sensitive nor specific. Diagnosis requires at least 15 eosinophils per high power field on oesophageal biopsy in a patient with symptoms of oesophageal dysfunction, and because the infiltrate is patchy and can spare the distal oesophagus, several biopsies are taken from both proximal and distal sites. Treatment options are a proton pump inhibitor, swallowed topical corticosteroid, or an elimination diet, with dilatation reserved for fibrostenotic strictures, and each is assessed by repeat histology rather than by symptoms alone.
key_points: Dietary adaptation over years often precedes the first bolus obstruction
Endoscopic rings and furrows are suggestive but not diagnostic
At least 15 eosinophils per high power field is the histological threshold
Patchy involvement means proximal and distal biopsies are both required
Acid suppression before biopsy can render the histology uninterpretable
explanation.pearls: Response to treatment in this condition is judged on repeat histology rather than on symptoms, because patients who feel better frequently have persistent mucosal eosinophilia that goes on to produce the fibrotic strictures responsible for long term dysphagia.

subtopic_detail: Eighteen months of dysphagia to solids and liquids together with regurgitation of undigested food and a normal endoscopy
stem:
You are the physician seeing a 52 year old woman with eighteen months of food sticking behind the sternum. She says it has been just as hard to get water down as bread from the very beginning, and that she has to stand up and arch her back to make things go through.

She brings up undigested food from hours earlier, sometimes onto her pillow, and has lost 6 kg. A proton pump inhibitor prescribed by her general practitioner made no difference. Endoscopy performed last week showed retained food and saliva in the oesophagus with a snug but passable gastro-oesophageal junction, normal mucosa and no mass, and gastric and duodenal biopsies were normal. A barium swallow shows a dilated oesophagus tapering smoothly to a narrow segment at the junction.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 21 kg per square metre having fallen from 23, chest clear on auscultation, abdomen soft and non tender, no supraclavicular lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, urea creatinine and electrolytes within normal limits, endoscopy shows retained food and saliva with normal mucosa, a passable gastro-oesophageal junction and no mass, gastric and duodenal biopsies normal, barium swallow shows a dilated oesophagus tapering smoothly at the junction

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Arrange high resolution oesophageal manometry to confirm the diagnosis
options.rationale: Dysphagia to solids and liquids from the outset with regurgitation of undigested food and a smoothly tapering junction on contrast study points to a motility disorder, and high resolution manometry is the diagnostic standard, demonstrating failure of relaxation of the lower oesophageal sphincter with absent peristalsis. Manometry also assigns the subtype, which determines which treatment is likely to work. (Source: GESA: Achalasia clinical update)

options.text: Start a proton pump inhibitor and review her symptoms in eight weeks
options.rationale: She has already had an adequate trial without benefit, which is expected because the obstruction is functional rather than acid related. Repeating an ineffective treatment delays the diagnosis while she continues to lose weight. (Source: GESA: Achalasia clinical update)

options.text: Refer for laparoscopic myotomy without further physiological testing
options.rationale: Manometric subtype predicts the response to myotomy, and operating without it risks a poor outcome in the subtype that responds least well. Definitive treatment follows rather than replaces the physiological diagnosis. (Source: GESA: Achalasia clinical update)

options.text: Arrange computed tomography of the chest and abdomen, then reassess
options.rationale: Weight loss and a narrowed junction do raise the possibility of a tumour producing the same picture, but endoscopy with a normal mucosa and normal biopsies has already addressed that. Imaging is added when the history is short, the patient older, or the endoscopist finds the junction difficult to traverse. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Achalasia)

options.text: Refer for oesophageal dilatation at the next available endoscopy list
options.rationale: Pneumatic dilatation is one of the definitive treatments but it carries a perforation risk and should not be undertaken before the diagnosis and subtype are established. The near pair here is a peptic stricture, where dilatation without manometry would be entirely appropriate. (Source: GESA: Achalasia clinical update)

explanation.summary: The single most useful discriminator in dysphagia is whether liquids are affected from the beginning, since a mechanical obstruction narrows progressively and therefore troubles solids first, whereas a motility disorder impairs transit of both from the outset. Achalasia results from loss of inhibitory neurons in the myenteric plexus, so the lower oesophageal sphincter fails to relax and peristalsis is lost, producing dysphagia, regurgitation of undigested food, chest pain and weight loss over months to years. Endoscopy is performed in every case to exclude pseudoachalasia, in which a tumour at the junction reproduces the picture, and a short history, older age or a junction that is difficult to pass should raise that suspicion. High resolution manometry confirms the diagnosis and classifies it into three subtypes, which matters because the subtype predicts response to pneumatic dilatation, laparoscopic myotomy and peroral endoscopic myotomy.
key_points: Dysphagia to liquids from the outset indicates a motility rather than mechanical cause
Failure to respond to acid suppression is expected in this condition
Endoscopy is mandatory to exclude a tumour mimicking the disorder
High resolution manometry is the diagnostic standard and assigns the subtype
Subtype predicts which definitive treatment is likely to succeed
explanation.pearls: Patients with achalasia carry a small but lifelong increased risk of oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma from chronic stasis, and this risk persists after successful myotomy, so new or changed dysphagia in a treated patient warrants repeat endoscopy rather than an assumption that the myotomy has failed.

subtopic_detail: An incidental immunoglobulin G kappa paraprotein of 12 g per litre with a normal free light chain ratio and normal end organ markers
stem:
You are the physician reviewing a 68 year old man referred after a paraprotein was found on blood tests ordered because of a raised total protein on a routine panel. He feels entirely well, walks 5 km most days and has kept his weight steady.

He reports no bone pain and no night sweats. On examination the lymph node areas, the abdomen and the axial skeleton are unremarkable, and pinprick and vibration sense are intact in both feet. Serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation identifies an immunoglobulin G kappa paraprotein of 12 g/L, the serum free light chain ratio is within the normal range, and his haemoglobin, calcium and creatinine are all normal.

data_table.Examination: No lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly, no bony tenderness, no peripheral neuropathy on testing pinprick and vibration sense, no macroglossia
data_table.Investigations: Immunoglobulin G kappa paraprotein 12 g/L, serum free light chain ratio within the normal range, haemoglobin 142 g/L (130 to 180), corrected calcium 2.34 mmol/L (2.20 to 2.60), creatinine 78 micromol/L (60 to 110), immunoglobulin A and immunoglobulin M within normal limits, urine protein electrophoresis shows no Bence Jones protein

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for bone marrow biopsy and skeletal survey before further review
options.rationale: Marrow examination and imaging are indicated when the paraprotein is 15 g/L or more, is not immunoglobulin G, or the free light chain ratio is abnormal, or where there is any evidence of end organ damage, none of which applies here. Investigating a low risk finding exposes him to an invasive procedure with a very low yield. (Source: HSANZ: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance position statement)
source_refs: HSANZ: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance position statement

options.text: Start bortezomib based therapy and refer to the haematology clinic
options.rationale: Treatment is directed at symptomatic myeloma defined by anaemia, hypercalcaemia, renal impairment or bone lesions, and he has none of these. Treating an asymptomatic paraprotein exposes him to toxicity without evidence of benefit. (Source: HSANZ: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance position statement)
source_refs: HSANZ: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance position statement

options.text: Arrange whole body magnetic resonance imaging and review in six months
options.rationale: Whole body imaging is used to detect occult bone disease in smouldering myeloma or where risk features are present, and it is not part of the assessment of a low risk paraprotein. The near pair here is a patient with the same paraprotein but bone pain, in whom imaging would be essential. (Source: HSANZ: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance position statement)
source_refs: HSANZ: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance position statement

options.text: Repeat the paraprotein, blood count and renal function in six months
options.rationale: An immunoglobulin G paraprotein below 15 g/L with a normal free light chain ratio and no end organ damage carries none of the three recognised risk factors, so this is low risk monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance and the management is surveillance without marrow examination. Repeating at six months confirms stability, after which the interval extends to annually, because the risk of progression is only about 1 per cent per year. (Source: HSANZ: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance position statement)
source_refs: HSANZ: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance position statement

options.text: Reassure him that no further monitoring of any kind will be needed
options.rationale: The risk of progression is low but it is cumulative and lifelong rather than disappearing with time, so discharge without surveillance is not appropriate. Patients who stop being monitored typically present later with established end organ damage. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance

explanation.summary: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance is present in around 3 per cent of people over 50 and rises steeply with age, so it is a common incidental finding rather than a rare one. Risk of progression to myeloma or a related disorder is stratified on three factors, namely a paraprotein of 15 g/L or more, a non immunoglobulin G isotype, and an abnormal serum free light chain ratio, with progression risk rising from about 1 per cent per year when none is present to substantially higher when all three are. Patients with no risk factors and no evidence of end organ damage do not need a bone marrow biopsy or skeletal imaging, and are monitored with periodic blood tests, whereas anyone with a risk factor or any suggestion of damage is referred for full staging. The end organ features that define myeloma are hypercalcaemia, renal impairment, anaemia and bone lesions, and any of them converts surveillance into urgent investigation.
key_points: Risk stratification uses paraprotein size, isotype and free light chain ratio
Low risk disease needs neither marrow biopsy nor skeletal imaging
Progression risk is about 1 per cent per year and is lifelong
Hypercalcaemia, renal impairment, anaemia or bone lesions define myeloma
Surveillance intervals lengthen once stability has been demonstrated
explanation.pearls: An immunoglobulin M paraprotein progresses to Waldenstrom macroglobulinaemia or lymphoma rather than to myeloma, so the isotype changes not only the risk but which disease is being watched for and therefore which symptoms are asked about at review.

sources.label: HSANZ: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance position statement
BMJ Best Practice: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance

subtopic_detail: A haematocrit of 0.58 with itching after a hot shower and a palpable spleen in a man whose oxygen saturation is normal
stem:
You are the physician seeing a 58 year old man referred because three separate blood counts over four months have shown a haemoglobin around 190 g/L. He mentions in passing that he has developed intense itching for about half an hour after a hot shower, which he has been treating with moisturiser.

He has never smoked, sleeps well without snoring and his partner has not noticed any pauses in his breathing. He is not on testosterone or any other medication. His oxygen saturation is 98 per cent breathing room air, both at rest and after walking briskly along the corridor. On examination his face is plethoric and the splenic edge is palpable 3 cm below the left costal margin.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72 beats per minute, blood pressure 148/88 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Plethoric facies, conjunctival suffusion, splenic edge palpable 3 cm below the left costal margin, no hepatomegaly, no clubbing, no cyanosis, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 192 g/L (130 to 180), haematocrit 0.58 (0.40 to 0.52), white cell count 13.4 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), platelets 512 x10^9/L (150 to 400), ferritin 18 micrograms/L (30 to 300), urea creatinine and electrolytes within normal limits, oxygen saturation 98 per cent at rest and on exertion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Arrange overnight oximetry on 2 consecutive nights and review the report
options.rationale: Nocturnal hypoxaemia is a genuine cause of secondary erythrocytosis but does not explain a raised white cell count, a raised platelet count or splenomegaly. He also has no snoring, no witnessed apnoeas and normal daytime saturations. (Source: HSANZ: Myeloproliferative neoplasms diagnosis and management)
source_refs: HSANZ: Myeloproliferative neoplasms diagnosis and management

options.text: Measure serum erythropoietin and test for the JAK2 V617F mutation
options.rationale: A raised haematocrit accompanied by leucocytosis, thrombocytosis, splenomegaly, aquagenic pruritus and a low ferritin points to a primary marrow disorder rather than a hypoxic drive, and a suppressed erythropoietin with the JAK2 V617F mutation confirms it. That mutation is present in around 95 per cent of cases, so the pair of tests both establishes the diagnosis and excludes the secondary causes in which erythropoietin is normal or raised. (Source: HSANZ: Myeloproliferative neoplasms diagnosis and management)
source_refs: HSANZ: Myeloproliferative neoplasms diagnosis and management

options.text: Arrange renal tract ultrasound and review once it has been reported
options.rationale: An erythropoietin secreting renal lesion is a rare secondary cause worth excluding when erythropoietin is inappropriately raised, but imaging before measuring the hormone inverts the sequence. It also would not account for the splenomegaly or the other cell lines. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Polycythaemia vera)

options.text: Start venesection of 450 mL and review his blood count in four weeks
options.rationale: Venesection is the mainstay of treatment once the diagnosis is made, and it is urgent where there is hyperviscosity or thrombosis, but starting it before the cause is established removes the diagnostic information the counts carry. The near pair here is a patient presenting with a thrombotic event, in whom venesection would proceed alongside the diagnostic testing. (Source: HSANZ: Myeloproliferative neoplasms diagnosis and management)
source_refs: HSANZ: Myeloproliferative neoplasms diagnosis and management

options.text: Repeat the full blood count in three months and review him after that
options.rationale: Three counts over four months have already established that the elevation is persistent rather than a transient or apparent change from dehydration. Further delay leaves him at ongoing thrombotic risk without a diagnosis. (Source: HSANZ: Myeloproliferative neoplasms diagnosis and management)
source_refs: HSANZ: Myeloproliferative neoplasms diagnosis and management

explanation.summary: A persistently raised haematocrit is separated into apparent erythrocytosis from a reduced plasma volume, secondary erythrocytosis driven by erythropoietin, and primary disease of the marrow. The clinical features that point to primary disease are involvement of more than one cell line, splenomegaly, aquagenic pruritus, and a low ferritin reflecting iron consumption by an expanded red cell mass in someone who is not bleeding. Testing a suppressed erythropoietin alongside JAK2 mutation analysis distinguishes these efficiently, since secondary causes such as chronic hypoxaemia, obstructive sleep apnoea, high altitude, smoking, testosterone use and erythropoietin secreting tumours all leave erythropoietin normal or raised. The clinical importance lies in thrombosis, which is the main cause of morbidity and death, and treatment combines venesection to a target haematocrit below 0.45, low dose aspirin, and cytoreduction for those at higher risk.
key_points: Involvement of more than one cell line argues against a secondary cause
A low ferritin without bleeding reflects consumption by an expanded red cell mass
Aquagenic pruritus is a characteristic and often overlooked symptom
Suppressed erythropoietin separates primary from secondary erythrocytosis
Thrombosis is the dominant clinical risk and drives treatment decisions
explanation.pearls: The target for venesection is a haematocrit below 0.45, and iron should not be replaced even though the ferritin falls, because iron deficiency is the mechanism by which venesection restrains red cell production.

sources.label: HSANZ: Myeloproliferative neoplasms diagnosis and management

subtopic_detail: An acutely hot swollen knee in a seventy six year old with chondrocalcinosis on radiograph and a temperature of 37.8 degrees
stem:
You are the physician called to see a 76 year old woman who developed a painful swollen right knee overnight. She has had two similar episodes in the past three years, each settling over a week or so with anti inflammatory tablets.

She takes hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension and has stage 3 chronic kidney disease. There has been no injury and no recent travel. The knee is warm, swollen and tense with a large effusion, and she will not let you flex it beyond 20 degrees. A radiograph taken in the emergency department shows fine linear calcification within the meniscal cartilage of both knees. Her temperature is 37.8 degrees Celsius.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 138/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 37.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Right knee warm and swollen with a tense effusion and patellar tap, flexion limited to 20 degrees by pain, overlying skin intact with no break or cellulitis, no other joint involved, no tophi
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 13.8 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), C reactive protein 118 mg/L (less than 5), serum urate 0.34 mmol/L (0.16 to 0.42), creatinine 128 micromol/L with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 42 mL/min/1.73m2, knee radiograph shows linear calcification of the meniscal cartilage in both knees

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Aspirate the joint for cell count, culture and polarised light microscopy
options.rationale: A hot swollen joint with fever and a C reactive protein of 118 must be sampled, because crystal arthritis and infection are clinically indistinguishable and can coexist, and the fluid provides the cell count, the Gram stain and culture, and the crystal identification in a single procedure. Aspiration also relieves the pressure of a tense effusion and is done before antibiotics wherever possible. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Start oral colchicine and review her again in forty eight hours
options.rationale: Colchicine is a reasonable treatment for the crystal arthritis suggested by the radiograph, but treating without sampling risks masking a septic joint that destroys cartilage within days. Her estimated glomerular filtration rate of 42 also requires dose reduction and makes toxicity more likely. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Start oral prednisolone and review her again in forty eight hours
options.rationale: Corticosteroid is effective for crystal arthritis in a patient with renal impairment, but giving it before the joint is sampled both obscures the diagnosis and would worsen an unrecognised infection. The near pair here is that this becomes the treatment of choice once infection has been excluded on the fluid. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Start intravenous flucloxacillin and review her response overnight
options.rationale: Antibiotics before aspiration substantially reduce the yield of synovial culture, leaving her on a prolonged empirical course with no organism and no drainage. Treatment for infection begins immediately after the sample is taken rather than instead of it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the knee and then reassess
options.rationale: Imaging cannot distinguish an infected effusion from a sterile inflammatory one, which is the question that must be answered tonight. It also delays a procedure that is both diagnostic and therapeutic. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease

explanation.summary: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease produces acute attacks that closely resemble gout, most often in the knee or wrist of an older patient, and chondrocalcinosis on a radiograph supports it but is a common incidental finding with age and does not prove that it is the cause of the current attack. The essential principle in any acutely hot swollen joint is that septic arthritis cannot be excluded clinically, that crystals and infection can coexist in the same joint, and that the joint is therefore aspirated before treatment. Synovial fluid is sent for cell count and differential, Gram stain and culture, and polarised light microscopy, where rhomboid weakly positively birefringent crystals identify pyrophosphate and needle shaped strongly negatively birefringent crystals identify urate. Treatment once infection is excluded is with a non steroidal anti inflammatory drug, colchicine or a corticosteroid given orally or into the joint, chosen according to comorbidity, and an underlying metabolic association such as haemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism or hypomagnesaemia should be considered in younger patients or polyarticular disease.
key_points: Chondrocalcinosis supports but does not prove crystal arthritis as the current cause
Crystal arthritis and septic arthritis can occur in the same joint
Aspiration answers the infective and the crystal question in one procedure
Antibiotics and corticosteroids both obscure the diagnosis if given first
Renal impairment restricts the choice of anti inflammatory treatment
explanation.pearls: Chondrocalcinosis appearing in a patient under 55, or affecting several joints, should prompt testing for haemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism and hypomagnesaemia, since in that age group the deposition is far more likely to be secondary to a metabolic disorder than age related.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease

subtopic_detail: A magnetic wide based gait with urinary urgency and ventriculomegaly out of proportion to cortical atrophy in a seventy four year old
stem:
You are the geriatrician seeing a 74 year old man whose wife says that over eighteen months he has begun to walk as though his feet are stuck to the floor, taking small shuffling steps and turning in several small movements rather than one.

He has had three falls and now uses a walking frame. He has started to reach the toilet too late, which distresses him greatly. His wife reports that he is slower to answer questions and has lost interest in the newspaper, but he still recognises visitors, manages his own medications with a dosette box and has had no visual hallucinations. There is no resting tremor and no rigidity, and his arm swing is preserved. Computed tomography of the brain reports enlarged lateral ventricles with an Evans index of 0.36 and only mild cortical sulcal widening.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits with no postural drop
data_table.Examination: Wide based short stepped gait with reduced foot clearance and en bloc turning, preserved arm swing, no resting tremor, no cogwheel rigidity, power and reflexes normal, plantar responses downgoing, Montreal Cognitive Assessment 23 out of 30 with losses in executive and attention items
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count urea creatinine and electrolytes within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, vitamin B12 and folate within normal limits, syphilis serology negative, computed tomography of the brain reports an Evans index of 0.36 with mild cortical sulcal widening

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Start a cholinesterase inhibitor and review his cognition in three months
options.rationale: Cholinesterase inhibitors are used in Alzheimer disease and in dementia with Lewy bodies, in which memory or visual hallucinations dominate and gait disturbance appears late. Here gait came first and the cognitive change is executive rather than amnestic. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Refer directly for ventriculoperitoneal shunt insertion without further tests
options.rationale: Only a proportion of patients with this radiological and clinical picture improve after shunting, and the operation carries risks of infection, subdural haemorrhage and shunt failure. Predicting response before committing to surgery is what the preliminary testing is for. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Start an anticholinergic for the urinary symptoms and review in three months
options.rationale: Treating the bladder in isolation addresses one element of a triad while leaving the gait and cognition untouched, and anticholinergic agents worsen cognition in an older patient with existing impairment. The near pair here is isolated overactive bladder without gait or cognitive change, where this would be reasonable. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Arrange a large volume lumbar puncture with gait assessment before and after
options.rationale: Removing 30 to 50 mL of cerebrospinal fluid and comparing timed gait measures before and afterwards is the standard way of predicting which patients will benefit from shunting, and a clear improvement identifies the group most likely to respond. Objective timed testing rather than global impression is used because the improvement can be modest and short lived. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Arrange carotid duplex ultrasound and review once it has been reported
options.rationale: Carotid imaging is directed at stroke risk in a patient with a territorial ischaemic event or carotid bruit, neither of which is present, and asymptomatic carotid disease would not produce this gradually progressive triad. It does not address the question being asked. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Normal pressure hydrocephalus)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Normal pressure hydrocephalus

explanation.summary: Normal pressure hydrocephalus presents with a triad of gait disturbance, urinary incontinence and cognitive impairment, and it matters disproportionately because it is one of the few causes of cognitive decline in older people that can be substantially improved by treatment. Gait is characteristically the first and most prominent feature, described as magnetic, wide based and short stepped with turning en bloc, and the pattern in which gait clearly precedes cognitive change is the most useful clinical discriminator from Alzheimer disease and from dementia with Lewy bodies. Imaging shows ventricular enlargement disproportionate to cortical atrophy, usually quantified by an Evans index above 0.3, but this appearance alone is neither sufficient nor specific. Selection for surgery therefore rests on demonstrating a response to cerebrospinal fluid removal, either by a high volume lumbar puncture with objective gait timing or by extended lumbar drainage, since gait is the domain most likely to improve after shunting while cognition responds least.
key_points: Gait disturbance precedes and dominates the cognitive change
The gait is wide based and magnetic with en bloc turning
An Evans index above 0.3 supports but does not establish the diagnosis
Response to cerebrospinal fluid removal predicts response to shunting
Gait improves most after shunting and cognition least
explanation.pearls: Preserved arm swing with a short stepped shuffling gait distinguishes this condition from Parkinson disease, where arm swing is reduced early, and it is the reason the gait has been described as a lower body parkinsonism that spares the upper limbs.

sources.label: Dementia Australia: Diagnosis and assessment of dementia
BMJ Best Practice: Normal pressure hydrocephalus
